outcome: Nothing published since 26 January 2024 settles, or moves a quantity in, the converse of Wolstenholme's theorem. Every in-window source I opened still treats the converse as open. The only in-window paper that names it (arXiv:2609.03091, 2 Sep 2026) restates it as an open conjecture with no new result. The one in-window item with AI involvement (arXiv:2604.16507, Lean formalisation) concerns the forward theorem, not the converse.
problem_asks: Yes/no: does the converse of Wolstenholme's theorem hold for all natural numbers? Unpacked: (1) Wolstenholme's theorem itself, that C(2p-1, p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p³) for every prime p ≥ 5, is background and is not asked. (2) The converse asked: every natural number n with C(2n-1, n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n³) is prime, equivalently no composite n satisfies the congruence. A full answer must cover every composite n, even and odd. (3) 'For all natural numbers' ranges over n = 1, 2, 3, ... . n = 1 satisfies the congruence (C(1,0) = 1 ≡ 1 mod 1) and is not prime. n = 2, 3, 4 do not satisfy it. So the bullet as frozen is false at n = 1 unless it is read with a lower bound such as n > 3 or n ≥ 5, as Jones's formulation in the literature has it; the bullet does not say so. I record this and leave the reading to the judging pass. (4) The question is one-directional: the forward statement is not asked.

events.what_happened: Charles Helou and Guy Terjanian, 'On Wolstenholme's theorem and its converse', Journal of Number Theory 128(3) (2008) 475-499, DOI 10.1016/j.jnt.2007.06.008. Establishes relations and congruences for w_n = C(2n-1, n-1) and deduces that the converse holds for many infinite families of composite n. The abstract states that the converse 'has been conjectured to be true, remains an open problem'. Print date March 2008; the DOI suffix suggests 2007 online. No earlier preprint found.
events.delivers: For the composite n in the infinite families the paper identifies, no n satisfies the mod-n³ congruence, so the converse holds there. The families are not listed in the sources I could read, and I did not read the full text. Restricted to those families; says nothing about other composites.
events.remains: The converse for all composite n outside those families, which is the general problem.

checked_by.who: Referees and editors of the Journal of Number Theory (Elsevier)
checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed number-theory journal; referees are anonymous and not named in the sources

events.direction: Partial, in favour of the converse: confirms it for infinitely many composite families and leaves the general case open. The paper itself calls the converse open.

events.what_happened: Vilmar Trevisan and Kenneth E. Weber, 'Testing the converse of Wolstenholme's theorem', Matemática Contemporânea 21 (2001) 275-286, from the 16th Escola de Álgebra in Brasília (2000). Reported result: for every even positive n, C(2n-1, n-1) is not ≡ 1 (mod n³). I did not open the paper itself (the UFRGS repository page returned a security-check error). The result is taken from the Meštrović survey (arXiv:1111.3057, which I opened), from Hussein's 2018 note, and from the OEIS A244214 comments.
events.delivers: No even composite n satisfies the mod-n³ congruence, so the converse holds for all even n. Restricted to even n.

checked_by.qualification: Number theorist publishing a survey of Wolstenholme-type congruences
checked_by.what_they_did: Reports the Trevisan-Weber result with a citation. The survey states no independent verification of the argument.

events.doubts: The result is known to me only from secondary reports. The primary text was not read.
events.direction: Supports the converse for even n.

events.what_happened: Richard J. McIntosh, 'On the converse of Wolstenholme's Theorem', Acta Arithmetica 71 (1995) 381-389, DOI 10.4064/aa-71-4-381-389. Secondary sources report that he verified the converse for all n < 10⁹ (Hussein 2018; the Meštrović survey; OEIS A244214, which cites McIntosh 1995 p. 387). He also conjectured that composites satisfying the weaker mod-n² congruence are exactly the squares of Wolstenholme primes, and that no prime satisfies the congruence mod p⁵. The IMPAN page gives metadata only and no abstract. I did not read the full text.
events.delivers: Numerical: no composite n < 10⁹ satisfies C(2n-1, n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n³). This is a finite-range check of a universal claim, so by the scope test it moves no quantity in the general problem. It is recorded as a finite instance check.

checked_by.who: R. J. McIntosh (the paper's author; the computation is his)
checked_by.qualification: Author of the paper and of the computation; method not read
checked_by.what_they_did: Computed C(2n-1, n-1) mod n³ for n < 10⁹ and reported no counterexample

events.directly_checkable: Anyone can recompute C(2n-1, n-1) mod n³ for n < 10⁹ with a computer algebra system. The OEIS entry gives code for small n and a b-file.
events.doubts: None raised in the sources I read. The computational method and the exact range are not described in the sources I read.
events.direction: Supports the converse in the range n < 10⁹: no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Kevin A. Broughan, Florian Luca and Igor E. Shparlinski, 'Some divisibility properties of binomial coefficients and the converse of Wolstenholme's theorem', Integers 10 (2010), no. 5, article A41, pp. 485-495, DOI 10.1515/INTEG.2010.041. Studies the weaker congruence C(2n-1, n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n), not mod n³. Bounds the composite n ≤ x satisfying it by x·exp(-(1/√2 + o(1))·√(log x log log x)), which is density zero. The bound comes from search-result abstract text; the page I opened gives metadata only.
events.delivers: For the mod-n variant, composite solutions up to x are density zero. This is an analogue, not the mod-n³ question. However, a mod-n³ solution is also a mod-n solution, so the mod-n³ composite solutions are a subset of this set and also have density zero. That does not show there are none.
events.remains: Whether any composite n satisfies the mod-n³ congruence. Density zero is compatible with existence.
events.direction: Density-zero bound for the mod-n version. Consistent with the converse, not decisive.

events.what_happened: Saud Hussein, 'A note on the converse of Wolstenholme's Theorem', arXiv:1806.05459, v1 14 June 2018, v2 16 October 2018. Proposition 4 (ar5iv HTML): for an odd prime p and a positive integer m with p^a < m < p^(a+1) < 2m, every n = m·p^b satisfies w_n ≢ 1 (mod n). That implies w_n ≢ 1 (mod n³). The abstract says the converse 'is shown to hold for the product m p^k'. I found no journal publication and no expert write-up.
events.revisions: v2 16 Oct 2018 (current per the arXiv abstract page)
events.delivers: The converse holds for the family n = m·p^k, for every m and odd prime p satisfying the inequality p^a < m < p^(a+1) < 2m. Restricted to that family and inequality.
events.remains: All composite n outside that family, including composites whose m fails the inequality and composites of other shapes.
events.doubts: Single-author preprint with no journal publication found. I read the ar5iv HTML rendering of Proposition 4 and did not check the proof line by line.
events.direction: Supports the converse on the stated family.

events.what_happened: Saud Hussein, 'New conjecture related to a conjecture of McIntosh', arXiv:1802.01909, submitted February 2018, v3 revised 17 July 2019. Restates Jones's converse as Conjecture 1.4 ('James P. Jones conjectures no other solutions exist'), notes it holds for even integers and prime powers up to 10⁹, and proposes Conjecture 2.7 on composites with C(2n-1, n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n²). Proves nothing about Conjecture 1.4.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. It restates the conjecture and adds a conjecture on the mod-n² variant.

events.what_happened: Romeo Meštrović, 'Wolstenholme's theorem: Its generalizations and extensions in the last hundred and fifty years (1862-2012)', arXiv:1111.3057, first submitted 13 Nov 2011, v2 dated 25 Dec 2011. A survey, not a result. It states that the converse, asked by J. P. Jones for many years, is 'still unanswered today', and records the McIntosh, Trevisan-Weber, Helou-Terjanian and Broughan-Luca-Shparlinski results.
events.delivers: No new result. A status statement only.
events.direction: No cut. Status record: open as of 2011.

events.what_happened: Christian Aebi, 'Wolstenholme and Morley, Primes and Pseudoprimes', arXiv:1306.2005, submitted 9 June 2013. Defines Wolstenholme pseudoprimes of order k, meaning composite odd n satisfying the congruence mod n^k for k = 1, 2, 3. Order 3 is the composite form of the converse. The abstract proves that p² is a Morley pseudoprime of order 2 iff a Wolstenholme pseudoprime of order 2 iff p is a Wolstenholme or Morley prime. It says only three non-prime-power order-1 pseudoprimes of Wolstenholme type are known. A v2 dated 26 Sep 2022 is a withdrawal whose page comment reads 'Unfinished and containing mistakes'. The abstract page does not mention the converse. One search snippet of the draft mentions a claim about twin primes, which I did not confirm.
events.delivers: Nothing on the order-3 (converse) case that I could read. The proved results concern order 2 and mod-p⁴ characterisations.
events.remains: All of the converse, including the order-3 composite case.
events.doubts: The author's own page comment says 'Unfinished and containing mistakes', and the paper was withdrawn in September 2022.

withdrawn.what: Paper withdrawn. The page comment reads 'Unfinished and containing mistakes'.
withdrawn.by: unknown; the arXiv v2 record shows the withdrawal

events.direction: No cut that I could establish. The withdrawn draft's order-3 content is not visible on the abstract page.

events.what_happened: Christian Aebi and Grant Cairns, 'Wolstenholme again', arXiv:1502.05750, submitted 19 Feb 2015. An elementary, self-contained proof that several Wolstenholme-type congruences attributed to Helou and Terjanian are equivalent. The abstract page does not mention the converse.
events.delivers: Equivalences among Wolstenholme-type congruences. Nothing on the converse.

events.what_happened: Jonathan Sondow, 'Extending Babbage's (Non-)Primality Tests', arXiv:1812.07650, submitted 18 Dec 2018. Revisits Babbage's 1819 criterion, which uses the mod-p² congruence for the binomial coefficient, and proves a partial converse to Babbage's non-primality test based on a single congruence. The abstract page does not mention Wolstenholme's converse. A search summary attributed to this paper the claim that 283686649 and 4514260853041 are composite counterexamples to Babbage's converse. I did not confirm that claim in the text, and the Hussein 1802.01909 page does not contain those numbers.
events.delivers: A partial converse to Babbage's non-primality test (a mod-m² criterion). This is a different question from Wolstenholme's converse.

events.what_happened: Zubeyir Cinkir, 'Beyond Wolstenholme's Theorem', arXiv:2312.10667. Posted 17 Dec 2023, before the window. v2 revised 21 Aug 2024, inside the window. Generalises Wolstenholme-type congruences modulo a prime p for sums of powers of residues and for products or ratios of terms. Sections 2 and 4 say computations were done in a reference [9], which I did not identify. The converse and Jones's conjecture are not mentioned in the text I read (about 100,000 of 106,423 characters).
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. Forward-type congruences modulo p.

events.what_happened: Gabriel Guedes and Ricardo Machado, 'Perfect numbers, Wieferich primes and the solutions of binom(2n,n) ≡ 2^n mod n'. Published online first in Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics 29(4) (2023) 705-712 on 16 Nov 2023, per the NNTDM landing page. The NNTDM PDF was not readable. Posted to arXiv as 2609.03091 on 2 Sep 2026 with the same title and abstract. Its Section 1 states Conjecture 1: 'If n > 3 and n³ | binom(2n-1, n-1) - 1 then n is a prime number'. It calls this 'Wolstenholme's converse problem', says it 'was proposed by J. P. Jones and remains open', and cites McIntosh for a check to 10⁹. The paper's own results concern binom(2n,n) ≡ 2^n (mod n). The NNTDM page lists 'Wolstenholme converse problem' as a keyword, so the 2023 version probably contains the same discussion. I did not confirm the Conjecture 1 text in the 2023 version.
events.revisions: arXiv:2609.03091 v1, 2 Sep 2026, same title and abstract, which gives the 2023 NNTDM journal reference. No later version seen.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. It restates Jones's conjecture, calls it open, and credits McIntosh's check to 10⁹.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 years since the 2023 online-first date
events.doubts: Restatement only, with no claim about the converse beyond attributing it to Jones and calling it open. The date depends on whether the 2023 version already contains Conjecture 1.
events.direction: No cut. An open conjecture restated.

events.what_happened: Gabriel Araújo Guedes and Ricardo Nunes Machado Junior, 'Structured Solutions of Prime-Base Binomial Congruences', arXiv:2606.30232, submitted 29 June 2026. Studies C(qn, n) ≡ q^n (mod n) for prime base q and the family n = q^t p. The abstract page does not mention Wolstenholme, the converse, Jones's conjecture, or AI.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. A different congruence.

events.what_happened: Nikita Kalinin, 'Wolstenholme's theorem over Gaussian integers', arXiv:2504.07978, submitted 30 Mar 2025. The arXiv page gives the journal reference Functiones et Approximatio Commentarii Mathematici 2025, pp. 1-11. Extends the forward theorem to the Gaussian integers. The abstract page says 'for a prime p > 7'; an aggregator said p > 5. Proposes conjectures linking to binomial coefficients and tabulates primes up to 1000. The converse and Jones's conjecture are not mentioned on the abstract page.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. A forward-type analogue over Z[i].

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal, per the arXiv journal reference
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per the arXiv journal reference)

events.doubts: The p > 7 versus p > 5 discrepancy is between the arXiv abstract and an aggregator. I did not read the full text.

events.what_happened: Jean-Christophe Pain, 'A proof of Wolstenholme's theorem and congruence properties via an Egorychev-type integral', arXiv:2604.03000, submitted 3 Apr 2026, single version. Gives a proof of the forward theorem and the mod-p⁴ refinement, and extracts the B_(p-3) term. The abstract page does not mention the converse or any AI tool.
events.delivers: The forward theorem, with a new proof. Not the converse.

events.what_happened: Alexandre Linhares, 'Deep Vision: A Formal Proof of Wolstenholme's Theorem in Lean 4', arXiv:2604.16507. v1 14 Apr 2026; v2 9 Aug 2026 (current). A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalisation, about 800 lines in nine lemmas, which the abstract says has no sorry declarations, of the forward theorem: C(2p, p) ≡ 2 (mod p³) for primes p ≥ 5. This is the bullet's forward form, since C(2p, p) = 2·C(2p-1, p-1). The abstract says the proof was found through 'a relational analogy engine for theorem proving and human-directed formalization'. The v1 HTML credits Claude Code and an LLM (Claude) with writing proofs. The converse appears only as background: §6.1 says 'McIntosh [25] investigated the converse direction, asking which composites satisfy the Wolstenholme congruence.' The paper does not formalise or claim the converse.
events.revisions: v2 9 Aug 2026 (current). I read the v1 HTML and the v2 abstract page only.
events.delivers: The forward theorem, formally verified in Lean 4 per the paper. Not the converse, and it does not touch composite n.
events.doubts: The sorry-free status is the author's claim in the abstract. I did not check the Lean code. The discovery credit goes to a system the authors call Deep Vision, and the proof-writing credit goes to Claude. Whether either is load-bearing for the forward theorem is for the judging pass to weigh. It does not bear on the converse.
events.direction: Forward theorem. Does not bear on the direction of the converse.

systems.name: Deep Vision
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, the proof was found through 'a relational analogy engine for theorem proving'. §4 calls Deep Vision 'an AI model to solve ARC-AGI problems'. §3.3 and §4.3 divide the work: 'machine for breadth, human for decomposition, LLM for depth'.
systems.basis_quote: a relational analogy engine for theorem proving and human-directed formalization

systems.name: Claude
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors (§3.3), an 'LLM formalization (Claude) that wrote the Finset manipulation proofs and number-theoretic arguments'. §4.2 says 'An LLM (Claude) writes the final proofs using the mathematical insight that the engine's structural matching cannot provide'. These are the authors' own words about formalisation and proof-writing.
systems.basis_quote: LLM formalization (Claude) that wrote the Finset manipulation proofs and number-theoretic arguments

systems.name: Claude Code
systems.what_it_did: An agent harness, not a model. The authors say 'The whole system runs on a laptop with access to Claude Code.' The model behind it is recorded as Claude above.
systems.basis_quote: The whole system runs on a laptop with access to Claude Code.

events.what_happened: Walid Kehila, Integers 26 (2026), article A32. Per a search summary (not the paper itself): received 28 Mar 2025, revised 9 Sep 2025, accepted 30 Jan 2026, published 20 Feb 2026. Uses an extended p-adic mean value theorem to refine Wolstenholme's theorem mod p⁷ for primes and introduces a family of binomial congruences. Not the converse. The full text was not read: the URL I tried returned binary data.
events.delivers: A forward refinement mod p⁷ for primes. Not the converse.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, per the search summary

events.doubts: Known only from a search summary. The date is the 2026 publication year, and an earlier preprint (2025 or early 2026) is possible but was not located.

events.what_happened: K. I. Pimenova, I. N. Faizov and I. B. Zhukova, 'On Gauss and Jacobsthal congruences', Chebyshevskii Sbornik 26(4) (2025) 174-182, DOI 10.22405/2226-8383-2025-26-4-174-182. Received 13 Jun 2025, accepted 17 Oct 2025, per a search summary. The summary says the paper extends the Wolstenholme-type congruence for the central binomial coefficient to composite moduli via the Jacobsthal congruence, giving a combinatorial proof of a weakened version. The summary does not say whether the composite-modulus statement is mod n or mod n³. If it is mod n³ for composite n, it would bear on the converse, so it needs reading. I did not open the paper (the m.math-net.ru page refused the connection).
events.delivers: Unverified. Per the summary, a composite-modulus analogue of the Wolstenholme congruence, which may or may not be a mod-n³ statement about composite n.
events.remains: Unverified. Possibly all of the converse.
events.doubts: Unread. A mod-n³ statement for composite n would conflict with the converse's direction, and that is implausible given the 10⁹ check, so the most likely reading is a weaker modulus. Not established.
events.direction: Unknown from what I could read.

events.what_happened: Armin Straub, 'Partial Lucas-type congruences', arXiv:2511.01174, submitted 2 Nov 2025 (listing) or 3 Nov 2025 (abstract page). Starts from a Chamberland-Dilcher binomial sum 'related to Wolstenholme's theorem' and proves partial Lucas congruences for constant terms of powers of Laurent polynomials. The converse and Jones's conjecture are not mentioned.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. A Lucas-type analogue of a Wolstenholme-related sum.

events.what_happened: Bo Jiang and Zhi-Wei Sun, 'On p-adic congruences involving √d', arXiv:2504.12242, submitted 16 Apr 2025. Congruences modulo p and p² for products and sums over m, n with p ∤ m² - dn², extending a conjecture of Kalinin. The paper describes a 'Wolstenholme-type congruence' but does not state the converse or Jones's conjecture.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. A quadratic-field analogue.

events.what_happened: Kevin Calderon, 'Ljunggren-Jacobsthal and Bailey-Type Congruences for Rectangular Gaussian Binomial Coefficients', arXiv:2608.00347, submitted 31 Jul 2026. Motivated by Kalinin's Gaussian analogue; proves a supercongruence for p > 5 in the inert-prime case of a conjecture of Kalinin. The converse is not mentioned.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. A Gaussian-integer analogue.

events.what_happened: Naoya Yamaguchi and Yuka Yamaguchi, 'Group Permanents of Abelian p-Groups and Young Diagrams', arXiv:2606.23765, submitted 22 Jun 2026. Counts monomials in group permanents and gives a criterion involving Wolstenholme primes. Neither the converse nor Jones's conjecture is mentioned.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. A criterion involving Wolstenholme primes, not the composite-n question.

events.what_happened: Jiang Zeng, 'Higher-Order Cyclotomic Congruences for q-Secant and Generalized q-Euler Numbers', arXiv:2608.05829, submitted 6 Aug 2026. Congruences modulo powers of (1+q) and [p]_q, with a 'q-Wolstenholme-type quotient'. The converse is not mentioned.
events.delivers: Nothing on the converse. A q-analogue.

summary: Searched 37 web queries, two arXiv listing queries (a 'Wolstenholme' search returning 48 title or abstract hits, and a converse-wording search returning zero), and one zbMATH query (HTTP 403, not usable). Every source I opened treats the converse as open: the Helou-Terjanian abstract (2008), the Meštrović survey (2011, 'still unanswered today'), Hussein's 2018 note and 2018/19 conjecture paper, the Guedes-Machado restatement (Conjecture 1, 'remains open'), the Wikipedia article on Wolstenholme's theorem (the converse is 'conjectured', with McIntosh cited), the OEIS A244214 comments ('No such counterexample is known'), and the Wikipedia list of unsolved problems, whose entry reads 'Does the converse of Wolstenholme's theorem hold for all natural numbers?'. Partial results: no even composite (Trevisan-Weber, as reported); no composite n below 10⁹ (McIntosh, as reported); the families of Helou-Terjanian and Hussein's Proposition 4 (n = m·p^b under p^a < m < p^(a+1) < 2m, which gives w_n ≢ 1 mod n). The Broughan-Luca-Shparlinski density bound concerns the mod-n variant, and a mod-n³ solution is also a mod-n solution, so it constrains the mod-n³ set but does not show it is empty. Wikipedia's order-1 'Wolstenholme pseudoprimes' (27173, 2001341, ...) are composite solutions of the mod-n analogue, not of the bullet's mod-n³ congruence. The in-window (after 26 Jan 2024) items are generalisations of the forward theorem or unrelated congruences, and none moves the converse. The one in-window item that names the converse, arXiv:2609.03091 (2 Sep 2026), restates it as an open Conjecture 1 with no new result. Its journal version is dated online-first 16 Nov 2023 by the NNTDM landing page, which is before the window. I could not read the 2023 text, so it is unconfirmed whether the restatement itself predates the window. The only AI involvement I found in the sources is arXiv:2604.16507 (Linhares, April 2026). It is a Lean 4 formalisation of the forward theorem, and the authors credit 'Deep Vision', 'Claude' and 'Claude Code' with discovery and proof-writing. It does not touch the converse, so I record it as an event but not as a converse result. For the converse itself, no source I found credits any AI system. Searches on AlphaEvolve, Gemini Deep Think, OpenAI and Erdős-problem AI coverage returned nothing that mentions the converse. The erdosproblems.com site was not opened. Close calls: (a) the restatement's date (2023 journal versus 2026 arXiv); (b) the literal 'for all natural numbers' fails at n = 1, which the bullet does not exclude; (c) the Hussein family result is a mod-n statement, so it covers the mod-n³ congruence only indirectly; (d) Pimenova et al. (2025) may concern composite moduli, which I could not read.
competing_reading: The strongest case against 'open' is that the partial results jointly cover a lot: every even n, every n < 10⁹, and infinite families of composites from Helou-Terjanian and Hussein. Nothing I read shows a general proof, and the families are not enumerated in what I could read. A literal reading of the frozen bullet ('for all natural numbers') is answered 'no' by n = 1, since 1 satisfies the congruence and is not prime. That reading is not what the literature studies, which uses n > 3 or n ≥ 5. Finally, the order-1 Wolstenholme pseudoprimes (27173, 2001341, 16024189487, ...) are composite solutions of the mod-n analogue. They are not counterexamples to the mod-n³ bullet, but a reader could conflate them.
what_would_settle_it: A proof of the converse, or a composite n with C(2n-1, n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n³), would settle the general question either way. Short of that: the full texts of Helou-Terjanian (families) and McIntosh 1995 (method and range), which would show how far the verified region reaches. The 2023 NNTDM text of Guedes-Machado, which would date the restatement. The full text of Pimenova et al. 2025, which would show whether the composite-modulus statement is mod n or mod n³. The v2 text of arXiv:2604.16507 and any author statement on what 'Deep Vision' and Claude did in the forward proof, which would settle the AI attribution for that event.

judgement.why: No event after 26 January 2024 touches the converse: every one is about the forward theorem, an analogue (Gaussian, quadratic, q-, Lucas-type), a different congruence, or (Pimenova) unread, so they are variant or none. The pre-snapshot results are partial: Trevisan-Weber (even n), Helou-Terjanian (families) and Hussein's Proposition 4 (n = m·p^k family) are cases; McIntosh's check to 10⁹ is instances; Broughan-Luca-Shparlinski's density bound on the mod-n set is read as a bound on the mod-n³ composite set. None is whole, so nothing pre-snapshot is resolved. The Guedes-Machado restatement is dated to its 2023 journal version but scores none either way. Linhares formalises and re-proves the known forward theorem, which is a different question. Its AI credits (Deep Vision finding the proof, Claude writing Lean proofs) are about formalising a known result, not mathematics in a result on this problem, so ai_role is none.
judgement.doubts: Read literally, the statement ('for all natural numbers') is false at n = 1. The literature uses n > 3, and I answered on that reading. Pimenova et al. 2025 was not read; if its composite-modulus statement were mod n³, it would bear on the converse. Linhares's AI role could be argued as generated for the forward proof, but that event is a variant and it is discarded either way.
